query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: High configurational entropy in near‐equiatomic multi-element nanoparticles is the key factor that preserves their structural and chemical stability under high-temperature catalytic and thermoelectric conditions. This entropy stabilization minimizes atomic diffusion and segregation, thereby maintaining a uniform solid‐solution despite service conditions that might otherwise promote phase separation.
generation.material_initial_state: Multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles produced via a rapid quenching method, which results in a homogeneously mixed atomic distribution at room temperature.
generation.intervention: Prepare a control batch using the standard rapid quench process to maintain high configurational entropy and an experimental batch that is subjected to a mild high-temperature annealing post-synthesis to promote partial atomic diffusion and elemental segregation.
generation.conditions: Thermal exposure in inert atmospheres within catalytic regimes (773–1173 K) and thermoelectric regimes (473–1923 K).
generation.structural_mediator: Degree of elemental homogeneity versus surface/sub-surface segregation and coarsening, as observed by atomic-scale compositional mapping and grain boundary analysis.
generation.mechanism: Rapid quenching locks in high configurational entropy, thereby creating a large free-energy barrier against atomic rearrangements that would otherwise lead to phase separation. In contrast, a controlled annealing treatment allows greater atomic mobility, reducing the entropy advantage and enabling diffusion-driven segregation and coarsening. This difference in microstructural evolution impacts the retention of catalytic active sites and thermoelectric conduction pathways.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles that retain high configurational entropy (control group) will exhibit less segregation, lower rates of coarsening, and maintain superior catalytic and thermoelectric performance compared with the annealed group, which is expected to show signs of phase separation and degradation of functional properties.
generation.baseline: Properties and stability expected from rapidly quenched nanoparticles synthesized under standard conditions, displaying uniform elemental mixing and minimal microstructural evolution under service conditions.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies when temperature-induced atomic mobility is moderate; at temperatures well above the stated ranges, even high entropy may not prevent phase separation. Additionally, effects related to particle size distribution or non-equiatomic compositions may fall outside this stabilizing mechanism.
generation.uncertainty: The relative contributions of kinetic factors (diffusivity, particle size effects) versus thermodynamic stabilization by configurational entropy remain to be quantitatively established. Variations in the rate of atomic diffusion among different element combinations also introduce uncertainty.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of nanoparticles: one using rapid quenching to preserve high configurational entropy, and one with a mild annealing step to induce controlled atomic mobility and segregation. Subject both batches to extended high-temperature aging tests within the specified service regimes under an inert atmosphere. Characterize their microstructure via TEM/EDS mapping and phase analysis (XRD) before and after aging, and measure changes in catalytic activity and thermoelectric properties.
measurements: Atomic-scale compositional mapping (e.g., EDS in TEM)
Catalytic activity (e.g., reaction rates, conversion efficiencies) before and after aging
Thermoelectric performance metrics (e.g., Seebeck coefficient, electrical conductivity)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the rapidly quenched nanoparticles do not show consistently lower levels of elemental segregation and coarsening—as well as better preservation of catalytic and thermoelectric performance—compared to the annealed nanoparticles, then the role of configurational entropy as the primary stabilizing mechanism is falsified.
